title: How would you design a system to send 1 million (or 100M) push notifications without overwhelming your servers — decouple generation from delivery via a queue, scale a worker fleet independently by queue depth, rate-limit to the provider (e.g. Firebase), make processing idempotent (unique notification ID), use provider batch APIs (1 request → N notifications), add retries → DLQ, generate campaign jobs progressively at very large scale, and track delivery through async provider callbacks?
shortTitle: How would you design a system to send 1 million (or 100M) push notifications without overwhelming your servers
topicTitle: How would you design a system to send 1 million (or 100M) push notifications wit

s1_definition.profdef: A large-scale push-notification system decouples generation from delivery through a queue so that producing the list of recipients never overwhelms the senders, scales a worker fleet independently based on queue depth, rate-limits outbound calls to the push provider such as Firebase so you stay within its limits, makes each notification idempotent with a unique notification id so retries and redeliveries do not double-send, uses the provider's batch API so one request delivers to many devices, retries transient failures and routes the permanently failed to a dead-letter queue, generates campaign jobs progressively rather than materialising hundreds of millions of rows at once, and tracks delivery state through the provider's asynchronous callbacks. The whole design turns a huge, bursty workload into a smooth, backpressured, horizontally scalable pipeline.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must text a hundred million customers about a new scheme. If one clerk tried to call everyone at once the branch would collapse. Instead the bank splits the job: one team writes names onto slips and drops them into a big in-tray, and a separate, resizable team of senders takes slips from the tray and sends messages at a steady, safe pace the phone network accepts, bundling many numbers into one dispatch where possible. Each slip has a unique ticket number so nobody is messaged twice even if a slip is re-processed, slips that fail are retried a few times and then set aside in a problem tray for review, the name-writers work through the list in chunks rather than printing a hundred million slips in one go, and delivery confirmations arrive later and are ticked off against the ticket numbers.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A large-scale push-notification system decouples generation from delivery through a queue so that producing the list of recipients never overwhelms the senders, scales a worker fleet independently based on queue depth, rate-limits outbound calls to the push provider such as Firebase so you stay within its limits, makes each notification idempotent with a unique notification id so retries and redeliveries do not double-send, uses the provider's batch API so one request delivers to many devices, retries transient failures and routes the permanently failed to a dead-letter queue, generates campaign jobs progressively rather than materialising hundreds of millions of rows at once, and tracks delivery state through the provider's asynchronous callbacks. The whole design turns a huge, bursty workload into a smooth, backpressured, horizontally scalable pipeline.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must text a hundred million customers about a new scheme. If one clerk tried to call everyone at once the branch would collapse. Instead the bank splits the job: one team writes names onto slips and drops them into a big in-tray, and a separate, resizable team of senders takes slips from the tray and sends messages at a steady, safe pace the phone network accepts, bundling many numbers into one dispatch where possible. Each slip has a unique ticket number so nobody is messaged twice even if a slip is re-processed, slips that fail are retried a few times and then set aside in a problem tray for review, the name-writers work through the list in chunks rather than printing a hundred million slips in one go, and delivery confirmations arrive later and are ticked off against the ticket numbers.

**One line to remember:** Send notifications at scale by decoupling generation from delivery with a queue, autoscaling workers by queue depth, rate-limiting and batching to the provider, making each notification idempotent by unique id, retrying to a dead-letter queue, generating campaign jobs progressively, and tracking delivery via async provider callbacks.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the core problem and the first principle that solves most of it: decoupling generation from delivery. Generating the recipient list, which might be a hundred million rows from a query, and actually delivering to the push provider are two very different workloads with very different rates, and if you try to do them in one synchronous flow, a burst of generation overwhelms your senders and the provider. So you put a durable queue between them. A generator produces notification jobs and enqueues them; a separate fleet of delivery workers consumes from the queue at whatever rate is sustainable. The queue is the shock absorber: generation can be bursty, the queue buffers, and delivery drains smoothly. This decoupling is the single most important design decision, because it converts a spiky, tightly-coupled process into a backpressured pipeline where neither side can overwhelm the other.

Scaling the worker fleet independently by queue depth is the next principle. Because delivery is separated, you can size the delivery fleet to the work, not to the generation rate. You autoscale the number of workers based on the queue depth or consumer lag: when the backlog grows, add workers; when it drains, remove them. This lets a hundred-million campaign be absorbed by temporarily scaling the fleet up and then back down, and it means your servers are never overwhelmed because the fleet size tracks the actual sustainable throughput rather than the instantaneous arrival rate.

Rate-limiting to the provider is essential because the push provider, like Firebase Cloud Messaging or APNs, enforces its own limits, and exceeding them gets you throttled or blocked. You apply a rate limiter, typically a token bucket sized to the provider's allowed rate, on the outbound path so the fleet never sends faster than the provider accepts. This protects both the provider relationship and your own system from the wasted work of rejected calls, and it means adding workers beyond the provider's rate simply makes them wait on the limiter rather than causing failures.

Idempotency with a unique notification id prevents double-sending, which matters because the pipeline is at-least-once: a worker might crash after sending but before acknowledging, so the message is redelivered and processed again, and transient retries can re-attempt a send. Each notification carries a unique id, and you record which ids have been successfully delivered, so a reprocessed job checks the id and skips if it was already sent. This turns at-least-once delivery into effectively exactly-once from the user's perspective, so customers are not spammed with duplicates.

Batch APIs multiply throughput for free. Providers offer batch or multicast endpoints where one request carries many device tokens, so instead of one HTTP call per notification you send one call per batch of, say, five hundred devices. This dramatically reduces the number of outbound requests, the per-request overhead, and the pressure on rate limits, so a worker batches the jobs it has pulled into provider-sized batches and sends them in one call. Batching is often the difference between needing a huge fleet and a modest one.

Retries with a dead-letter queue handle failures without losing or blocking on them. Transient failures, a timeout or a temporary provider error, are retried with backoff, ideally only for the devices in a batch that actually failed, since batch responses report per-token results. A notification that keeps failing after a bounded number of retries, or fails permanently because a device token is invalid or unregistered, is moved to a dead-letter queue instead of retried forever, so it does not block the pipeline, and a separate process inspects the dead-letter queue to clean up stale tokens or investigate. Invalid-token responses also feed back to prune your token store.

Progressive campaign generation is specific to the very large scale, a hundred million. You do not materialise a hundred million jobs in one burst, because that itself would overwhelm the queue, memory, and database. Instead the generator produces jobs progressively, paginating through the recipient set in chunks and enqueuing a manageable number at a time, pacing itself to the queue's capacity and the fleet's drain rate. This keeps the queue bounded and the whole system smooth even for enormous campaigns, and it lets you pause, resume, or cancel a campaign mid-flight.

Delivery tracking uses asynchronous provider callbacks because you do not know the final outcome at send time. The provider accepts the request quickly but actual delivery to the device, and whether it was opened, is reported later through callbacks or webhooks, or you poll a receipts API. You consume these asynchronously and update each notification's state, sent, delivered, opened, or failed, keyed by the unique id, so you have accurate per-notification status and campaign-level metrics without blocking the send path waiting for confirmation. This also feeds retries, since a reported failure can trigger a resend, and analytics.

Senior nuances worth stating: use a partitioned queue like Kafka so delivery workers scale out by partition and ordering is preserved per key; separate priority streams so time-critical notifications are not stuck behind a bulk campaign; make the generator checkpoint its progress so a crash resumes rather than restarts; prune invalid tokens from provider feedback to keep the list clean; cache nothing sensitive and respect user notification preferences and quiet hours in the generator; and monitor queue depth, provider error rate, and delivery-success rate as first-class signals. The through-line is that the queue plus independent worker scaling plus provider rate-limiting and batching is what makes a hundred million notifications a smooth background job rather than an outage.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wanted to push a scheme announcement to a hundred million customers, and an early attempt generated and sent synchronously, instantly overwhelming the senders and the provider. This is exactly the coupling problem, solved by putting a durable queue between generation and delivery so neither side overwhelms the other.

Problem 2 — The provider, Firebase, throttled the bank for sending too fast, and duplicate sends annoyed customers when workers retried after crashes. This is exactly the rate-limit and idempotency problem, solved by a token-bucket limiter on the outbound path and a unique notification id recorded on success so retries skip already-sent messages.

Problem 3 — Sending one request per customer was far too slow, and permanently failing tokens kept retrying forever. This is exactly the batching and dead-letter problem, solved by using the provider's batch API and routing exhausted or invalid sends to a dead-letter queue.

Our mini-project builds a notification-pipeline core. The code generates campaign jobs progressively into a queue, has workers that batch, rate-limit, idempotently send, retry transient failures, and dead-letter permanent ones, and updates delivery state from simulated async callbacks. The demo runs a scheme-announcement campaign including Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a scheme-announcement campaign to six device tokens including Rajesh, Priya, and one invalid token, which stands in for a hundred-million-recipient campaign.

Step 1: The campaign generator pages through the recipient list in chunks rather than materialising all of them at once, and for each recipient it creates a job with a unique notification id derived from the campaign id and the token, then enqueues it. Generation is bursty but the queue absorbs it, and because it is progressive the queue never balloons. This is the decoupling that keeps the senders from being overwhelmed.

Step 2: The delivery worker drains the queue. It checks each job's unique id against its sent store; none are sent yet, so all proceed. This idempotency check is what will later prevent double-sends on retries.

Step 3: The worker accumulates jobs into a batch up to the provider's batch size. When the batch is full or the queue empties, it sends the whole batch in one provider request, so one HTTP call delivers to many devices, which is the batching that multiplies throughput and relieves the rate limit.

Step 4: Before sending, the worker consumes a token from its rate-limiter bucket sized to the provider's allowed rate, so it never sends faster than Firebase accepts. If the bucket is empty, the worker waits for refill rather than causing rejections.

Step 5: The provider returns per-token results. Rajesh's and Priya's tokens succeed, so their notification ids are recorded as sent in the idempotency store and their state is marked sent. The invalid token fails in the batch response.

Step 6: For the failed invalid token, the worker retries a bounded number of times; it keeps failing because the token is permanently invalid, so after exhausting retries the worker routes it to the dead-letter queue and marks it failed, instead of retrying forever and blocking the pipeline. In production this also prunes the invalid token from the store.

Step 7: Later, asynchronous provider callbacks arrive reporting that Rajesh's notification was delivered and Priya's was opened. The tracker updates their state keyed by token, giving accurate per-notification status and campaign metrics without the send path ever having waited for confirmation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To send a million or a hundred million push notifications without overwhelming my servers, the single most important decision is to decouple generation from delivery with a durable queue. Producing the recipient list and delivering to the provider are completely different workloads at different rates, so I put a queue between them: a generator enqueues notification jobs and a separate fleet of delivery workers drains them at a sustainable rate. The queue is the shock absorber that turns a spiky, tightly-coupled process into a backpressured pipeline where neither side can overwhelm the other.

From there I scale the delivery fleet independently by queue depth, adding workers when the backlog grows and removing them when it drains, so the fleet tracks actual sustainable throughput rather than the instantaneous arrival rate. I rate-limit the outbound path with a token bucket sized to the provider's limits, like Firebase or APNs, so the fleet never sends faster than the provider accepts and extra workers simply wait rather than causing rejections. I make each notification idempotent with a unique id and record which ids were delivered, so the at-least-once pipeline, where a worker can crash after sending but before acknowledging, becomes effectively exactly-once and customers are not spammed with duplicates. I use the provider's batch API so one request carries many device tokens, which dramatically cuts the number of outbound calls and the pressure on the rate limit, often the difference between a huge fleet and a modest one.

I handle failures with retries and a dead-letter queue: transient failures are retried with backoff, ideally only for the devices in a batch that failed since batch responses are per-token, and anything that keeps failing or is permanently invalid goes to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying forever, which also feeds token cleanup. For the very large scale I generate campaign jobs progressively, paginating the recipient set and enqueuing a manageable number at a time so the queue stays bounded and I can pause, resume, or cancel. And because I do not know the final outcome at send time, I track delivery through the provider's asynchronous callbacks, updating each notification's state, sent, delivered, opened, or failed, keyed by its unique id, so I get accurate status and campaign metrics without the send path ever blocking on confirmation.

On my project at National Bank of India an early scheme-announcement attempt generated and sent synchronously and instantly overwhelmed the senders and got us throttled by Firebase, with duplicate sends annoying customers after worker crashes. We rebuilt it as this pipeline: a progressive generator feeding a partitioned queue, an autoscaled worker fleet that batched into provider multicast requests under a token-bucket limiter, a unique notification id so retries skipped already-sent messages, a dead-letter queue for invalid tokens, and a tracker fed by async callbacks. After that a hundred-million campaign became a smooth background job that scaled the fleet up and back down, never overwhelmed our servers or the provider, and gave us precise per-notification delivery status. The nuance I add is to keep a separate priority stream so time-critical notifications are never stuck behind a bulk blast.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I send notifications at scale by decoupling generation from delivery with a queue, autoscaling workers by queue depth, rate-limiting and batching to the provider, making each notification idempotent by unique id, retrying transient failures to a dead-letter queue, generating campaign jobs progressively, and tracking delivery through asynchronous provider callbacks, which together turn a hundred million sends into a smooth, backpressured pipeline.
